title: Haunt / Spirit Manifestation (d100)
note: An OBSERVABLE phenomenon of the season of ghosts — what a PC actually perceives, never the GM-ONLY creature behind it. Surface the read only; do NOT name nindoru, noppera-bo, gwishin, Kugaptee, the mindscape, or any secret. Many phenomena echo the Eight Practices (don't whistle at night, don't leave laundry out, don't turn when called from behind, etc.). In town it's eerie unease; in the haunted hinterlands it's sharper. Whether these are 'really' ghosts is hotly debated, and locals won't call a ghost a ghost (Practice 1). The GM may privately tie a result to an actual creature/haunt, but the player learns only through investigation.

entries.value: A voice calls your name from directly behind you in the dark — but no one is there when you (against all advice) turn around.
Whistling answers your own whistle at night, from somewhere just past the lantern-light, pitch-perfect and a half-beat too slow.
Laundry left out overnight comes back faintly warm, smelling of someone else, and folded in a way no one in the house folds.
Cold spots that drift through a warm room; breath fogs indoors for three heartbeats, then it's gone.
Footsteps pace the floor above (or the path behind) in perfect time with yours, stopping the instant you stop.
A reflection in still water, a window, or a polished kettle lags behind you, or shows a face that isn't quite yours.
A familiar neighbor seen from behind — right clothes, right walk — who is somewhere else entirely when you find them, or who never turns to show a face.
Wet footprints lead from the river's edge into a home and simply stop in the middle of a dry room.
A lantern or candle gutters and dies though there's no draft; relighting it is strangely hard, and the dark that follows feels thicker than it should.
Doors and sliding screens that were shut stand open; ones that were open are shut and won't budge until you look away.
Soft weeping or a lullaby drifts from an empty room, a closed shop, or the trees — tender, grieving, and impossible to locate.
An offering bowl, grave-urn, or shrine has been disturbed: food eaten, incense relit, an item moved, no tracks.
A pale moth or a single blood-red butterfly settles on you out of season and will not be brushed away; more gather if you watch too long.
You feel a hand pat your head or shoulder from behind (Practice 2 broken) — and a chill where the fingers touched lingers for an hour.
Food on the table has two stick-like objects standing upright in it (Practice 4), and no one will admit to putting them there.
A figure leans against a sunlit wall at midday (Practice 5) where there was no one; the plaster there is cold and slightly damp.
Animals balk, bristle, and stare fixedly at an empty corner or a stretch of road; dogs whine, cats arch, livestock won't pass.
An object goes missing in plain sight, then turns up in an impossible place — inside a sealed jar, atop a beam, under a sleeper's pillow.
A child, or a person, briefly forgets their own name, the way home, or who a loved one is — the lapse passing like a cloud.
Mirror Lake, a rain-barrel, or the river runs unnaturally still and dark; something seems to watch from just under the surface (do not enter water near a ghost, Practice 3).
A smell that doesn't belong — funeral incense, river-rot, scorched hair, or a dead relative's perfume — fills a place and then vanishes.
The temperature, the light, and the birdsong all drop at once into a held, listening silence, as if the world is waiting for something.
A grave, urn, or coffin seems subtly wrong — lid ajar, soil disturbed, a faint sound from within — though nothing visible has changed.
Whispered conversation in an empty room cuts off the moment you enter; the air smells of stale breath that doesn't breathe.
A trusted face flickers — for an instant it has no features at all — then it's normal again and they act as if nothing happened.
Out in the hinterlands the path you walked unspools differently behind you; landmarks shift, and you've lost more time than you should have.
Tall grass, thatch, or a scarecrow-bundle by the road rustles against the wind and seems, for a heartbeat, to giggle or lean toward you.
An abandoned house feels lived-in — fire banked, tea warm, a place set for you — and grows quietly insistent that you stay the night.
A crane (or other wild creature) appears and watches you with uncanny calm; locals say seeing one is good luck — killing one, very bad.
Wood warps, weeps sap, or groans like a voice; meanwhile metal in the room tarnishes, frosts, or sings a thin note (the wood-vs-metal unease).
Cold fingers brush the back of your neck and a stranger's despair floods you — grief, regret, a death that isn't yours — passing in moments.
A pet, stray, or wild animal behaves with unsettling, almost human purpose — fixing you with a too-knowing stare, leading you somewhere.
Paper shuriken, fulu charms, or salt lines appear at a threshold overnight; someone in town is warding hard against something they won't name.
GM's choice / escalation: weave two of the above together, or let the dread point pointedly at the current scene's location or NPC.
